title: Scope.REQUEST: Propagation Overhead & Transient Provider Instances
prerequisites: Singleton vs Request vs Transient Scopes

progressiveExplaining.eli5: In standard NestJS, services are built once when the server boots up (like buying a single coffee machine for the whole office). When you use `Scope.REQUEST`, NestJS throws away the machine and builds a brand-new coffee machine from scratch for every single customer request, which slows down the server and burns memory.
progressiveExplaining.junior: NestJS providers have three injection scopes: `DEFAULT` (singleton created once at startup), `REQUEST` (a new instance is created for every incoming request and garbage collected after), and `TRANSIENT` (a new instance per injection site). You set it via `@Injectable({ scope: Scope.REQUEST })`. Because `REQUEST` scope re-instantiates services on every HTTP call, it significantly degrades throughput (can drop RPS by 30-50%).
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Request Scope suffers from **Scope Bubbling (Scope Infection)**: if a low-level service (e.g. `TenancyService`) is marked `Scope.REQUEST`, every service and controller that injects it is automatically forced into `Scope.REQUEST` up the entire dependency tree. This turns the entire controller hierarchy into ephemeral, per-request allocations, causing severe V8 garbage collection churn and latency spikes under high load.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: When a controller is `Scope.REQUEST`, NestJS's `ContextIdFactory` creates a unique `ContextId` for each incoming request. The `Injector` creates an ephemeral sub-container tree and evaluates constructors for all providers in that branch. After the response finishes, the entire sub-tree is unreferenced, forcing V8's Scavenger and Mark-Sweep GC to continuously collect thousands of short-lived class instances.

interviewGotchas.question: What is 'Scope Bubbling' (Scope Infection) in NestJS?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of how dependency injection scopes propagate.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Scope Bubbling means that **a provider's scope bubbles up the dependency chain**. If Service C is `Scope.REQUEST`, and Service B injects Service C, Service B *must* also become `Scope.REQUEST`. If Controller A injects Service B, Controller A also becomes `Scope.REQUEST`. A single request-scoped service at the bottom of the graph forces all dependent ancestors to be re-created on every request.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Do not assume that making only a database service request-scoped will leave your controllers as singletons; the entire tree above it becomes request-scoped.

interviewGotchas.question: How can you achieve multi-tenancy without using `Scope.REQUEST`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks performance-oriented architecture design for enterprise applications.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Use **Node.js `AsyncLocalStorage`** in an authentication middleware to store the tenant context for the asynchronous execution chain. Keep all NestJS services and controllers as `DEFAULT` (singletons). When database queries run, the singleton repository reads the active tenant ID from `AsyncLocalStorage.getStore()` without any DI re-instantiation overhead.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Migrating from `Scope.REQUEST` to `AsyncLocalStorage` often results in a 3x to 5x throughput improvement in benchmarks.
